title: Google (Gmail), Email sender guidelines (bulk-sender requirements)
text:
## Google Email Sender Guidelines: Bulk Sender Requirements

Starting February 1, 2024, Gmail enforced new requirements. A sender that sends close to 5,000 messages or more per day to personal Gmail accounts is treated as a bulk sender and must meet stricter rules.

## Authentication requirements for bulk senders

All three authentication methods are required. Set up SPF and DKIM email authentication for your domain. Set up DMARC email authentication for your sending domain; the enforcement policy can be set to p=none but the record must exist. The DKIM key length must be at least 1024 bits; a 2048-bit key is recommended for security.

## Spam rate monitoring

Keep the reported spam rate in Google Postmaster Tools below 0.10%. Avoid ever reaching a spam rate of 0.30% or higher. Reaching 0.30% or higher can cause delivery problems that are hard to reverse, so the practical target is well under 0.10%.

## Infrastructure requirements

Ensure that sending domains or IPs have valid forward and reverse DNS records (PTR records). The reverse DNS lookup (PTR) must match the sending IP, and the forward DNS (A/AAAA) must resolve back to the same IP. Use a TLS connection for transmitting email.

## Subscription and one-click unsubscribe

For marketing and subscribed messages, one-click unsubscribe is mandatory. Include the header List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click, and include the header List-Unsubscribe: <https://[domain]/unsubscribe/[path]>. This references RFC 8058 for the technical specification. Also include a clearly visible unsubscribe link in the message body. Senders must process unsubscribe requests within 2 days.

## Message formatting standards

Messages must comply with RFC 5322 (Internet Message Format). HTML must follow HTML standards. From: headers should include only one email address. Every message requires a valid Message-ID. Single-instance headers (From, To, Subject, Date) must appear only once. Do not impersonate Gmail From: headers.

## Domain alignment

For direct email, the domain in the sender's From: header must be aligned with either the SPF domain or the DKIM domain. This is the DMARC alignment requirement: at least one of SPF or DKIM must both pass and align with the visible From domain.

title: DMARC.org, DMARC Overview
text:
## What DMARC Is

DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) is an email authentication protocol designed to address limitations in SPF and DKIM adoption. The initiative emerged from PayPal's 2007 collaboration with Yahoo! Mail and Gmail, which demonstrated that sender-receiver information sharing could effectively reduce fraudulent emails.

## Core problems DMARC solves

The specification addresses four challenges: complex sender environments with multiple systems prevent universal authentication; mixed authenticated and unauthenticated message streams confuse receivers; senders lack feedback on authentication deployment effectiveness; and receivers hesitate to reject unauthenticated messages due to uncertainty.

## How it works: the alignment concept

DMARC determines if a message aligns with sender information the receiver already knows. It evaluates SPF and DKIM results to determine alignment and provides guidance for handling non-aligned messages. Alignment means the domain that passed SPF or DKIM matches the domain in the visible From: header.

## The three policy modes

DMARC records specify policies through the p= tag. p=none is monitoring mode, requesting data reports without enforcement. p=quarantine recommends isolating suspicious messages (often to spam/junk). p=reject instructs receivers to refuse non-aligned mail outright.

## Reporting components

DMARC supports two reporting types via DNS record tags. Aggregate reports (rua=) provide summary statistics about authentication results. Forensic reports (ruf=) provide detailed information about individual failed messages.

## Technical record structure

DMARC policies publish as DNS TXT records using tag-value syntax. Key tags include v=DMARC1 (protocol version), pct= (percentage of messages the policy is applied to), adkim= (DKIM alignment mode: s for strict, r for relaxed), aspf= (SPF alignment mode: s for strict, r for relaxed), and sp= (subdomain policy).

## Deployment strategy

The recommended five-step rollout: deploy DKIM and SPF foundations; align mailer identifiers appropriately; publish DMARC with p=none for data collection; analyze reports and adjust mail streams; gradually transition policies from none to quarantine to reject.

## Relationship to SPF and DKIM

DMARC builds upon these existing protocols, replacing the older ADSP while adding support for wildcarding, subdomain policies, slow rollout percentages, and quarantining capabilities.

title: Yahoo Inc (Yahoo/AOL), Sender Best Practices and 2024 Requirements
text:
## Enforcement timeline

Beginning in February 2024, Yahoo enforces the following sending standards.

## Authentication requirements

All senders must implement SPF or DKIM at a minimum. Bulk senders must implement both SPF and DKIM, publish a valid DMARC policy with at least p=none (DMARC must pass), use a DKIM key of at least 1024 bits, and ensure the domain in the From: header is aligned with either the SPF domain or the DKIM domain. ARC (Authenticated Received Chain) implementation is recommended for forwarded emails so that authentication survives intermediaries such as mailing lists.

## Spam complaint threshold

Keep your spam rate below 0.3%. This applies to all senders and bulk senders alike, and the rate is calculated based on mail delivered to the inbox. Staying well under this threshold, ideally under 0.1%, is the safer operating point.

## Unsubscribe requirements for bulk senders

Implement a functioning List-Unsubscribe header that supports one-click unsubscribe. The Post method (RFC 8058) is highly recommended. Have a clearly visible unsubscribe link in the email body. Honor unsubscribes within 2 days.

## Consent and permission standards

Send only to users who specifically requested it. Avoid purchasing mailing lists. Do not use auto-checked opt-in checkboxes. Implement a double opt-in confirmation process. Set clear recipient expectations about frequency and content at the point of signup.

## List hygiene requirements

Monitor hard bounces, soft bounces, and inactive recipients. Remove invalid recipients from your list promptly. Enroll in the Complaint Feedback Loop (CFL) for DKIM-signed mail so that spam complaints are reported back to you. Consider periodic reconfirmation emails for inactive subscribers.

## Other requirements

Maintain valid forward and reverse DNS records. RFC 5321 and RFC 5322 compliance is mandatory. Adhere to the CAN-SPAM Act.

title: IETF RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF) version 1
text:
## Core purpose

SPF enables domain administrators to authorize which mail servers can send email using their domain names. Administrative Management Domains (ADMDs) can explicitly authorize the hosts that are allowed to use their domain names, and a receiving host can check such authorization.

## Key mechanism: the MAIL FROM domain

SPF validates the domain in the SMTP reverse-path (MAIL FROM), the identity of the sender used when the transaction starts with a MAIL command that gives the sender identification. This is the envelope sender (return-path), which is distinct from the visible From: header. Because SPF checks the envelope and DMARC checks the visible From, SPF can pass while still failing DMARC alignment.

## DNS record format

SPF policies are published as DNS TXT records beginning with v=spf1. A typical record: v=spf1 +mx a:colo.example.com/28 -all. The record must contain exactly this version string to be recognized.

## Mechanisms

all (always matches, used for the default policy); include (recursively checks another domain's SPF record); a and mx (match if the sender IP is in the domain's A or MX records); ip4 and ip6 (direct IP address or CIDR range matching); exists (performs a DNS A lookup on a constructed name); ptr (reverse DNS validation, deprecated and not recommended).

## Qualifiers

Each mechanism takes an optional qualifier prefix: + (default) is pass; - is fail; ~ is softfail; ? is neutral. A common ending is -all (hard fail everything else) or ~all (softfail).

## Critical DNS lookup limit

SPF implementations MUST limit the total number of terms requiring DNS lookups to 10 during SPF evaluation, to avoid unreasonable load on the DNS. This applies to include, a, mx, ptr, exists, and the redirect modifier. Exceeding this limit produces a permerror. This 10-lookup cap is the single most common cause of SPF breakage as senders add third-party services.

## Result codes

SPF evaluation returns one of seven outcomes: pass (client authorized), fail (client explicitly not authorized), softfail (host probably not authorized), neutral (domain makes no assertion), none (no SPF record found or domain malformed), temperror (transient DNS error), permerror (record has syntax errors or is uninterpretable). Receivers should check HELO and MAIL FROM identities.

title: IETF RFC 6376, DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Signatures
text:
## What DKIM is

DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) is an email authentication mechanism that permits a person, role, or organization to claim some responsibility for a message by associating a domain with the message. It separates the message signer's identity from the purported author, using cryptographic signatures validated through DNS queries rather than certificate authorities. Unlike SPF, a valid DKIM signature survives forwarding because it travels inside the message itself.

## The DKIM-Signature header

The signature is embedded as a DKIM-Signature header field containing tag-value pairs. This header contains all of the signature and key-fetching data needed to verify the message.

## Signing Domain Identifier (SDID / d= tag)

The d= tag identifies the responsible domain. It must be a valid DNS name under which the DKIM key record is published. For DMARC, the d= domain must align with the visible From domain.

## Selector (s= tag)

Selectors subdivide the key namespace, enabling multiple concurrent keys per domain. They support key rotation and delegated signing authority. The verifier constructs the DNS query as [selector]._domainkey.[domain].

## Body hash (bh= tag)

The bh= tag is a base64-encoded hash of the canonicalized message body, preventing signature reuse across different messages. If the body is altered in transit, the body hash no longer matches and DKIM fails.

## Signed header fields (h= tag)

The h= tag is a colon-separated list specifying which headers are included in the signature calculation, in order. Only listed headers are protected.

## Public key retrieval

The verifier queries DNS TXT records in the _domainkey namespace using the pattern [selector]._domainkey.[domain]. The key record contains the public key (p= tag) and metadata such as acceptable hash algorithms and service type constraints. Recommended key length is 1024 bits minimum, with 2048 bits preferred.

title: Litmus, Email Analytics: How to Measure Email Marketing Success Beyond Open Rate
text:
## Why open rate is now unreliable

Apple Mail Privacy Protection (MPP) accounts for 55% of all opens as of March 2024. Open rate has become a challenging metric to look at on its own because the data is not there: MPP pre-fetches (loads) the tracking pixel and images the moment mail is delivered to an Apple Mail client, regardless of whether the recipient actually opened it, so it hides the subscriber IP address and artificially inflates the reported open count. Despite this, 40% of email marketers still turn to open rate as a primary measurement of success. Open rate remains useful only for relative comparison inside the same audience (for example A/B testing subject lines), not as a trustworthy absolute number.

## Recommended metrics and formulas

Click-through rate (CTR): (number of emails clicked / number of emails delivered) x 100. Measures how many delivered emails earned a click.

Click-to-open rate (CTOR): clicks divided by opens; because it is anchored to opens it is distorted by MPP, so many teams now favor CTR over CTOR.

Conversion rate: (number of conversions / number of emails delivered) x 100. Tracks the real action taken (purchase, signup, download, reply).

Unsubscribe rate: (number of unsubscribes / number of emails delivered) x 100. Indicates how well campaigns match subscriber preferences.

Revenue per email (RPE): revenue generated / number of emails delivered. Direct monetary value per send.

Subscriber lifetime value (LTV): monthly revenue per subscriber x average months on list.

Return on investment (ROI): (email revenue minus email marketing cost) / email marketing cost. Litmus cites an average email ROI of 36:1.

## Key insight

Revenue was cited as the primary goal by most email marketers surveyed, yet 72% do not know their email marketing ROI despite calling email their most effective channel. The practical shift post-MPP: measure clicks, conversions, and revenue, and treat opens as directional only.

title: US FTC, The CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business
text:
## What CAN-SPAM covers

The CAN-SPAM Act sets the rules for commercial email, establishes requirements for commercial messages, gives recipients the right to have you stop emailing them, and spells out tough penalties for violations. It covers all commercial messages, defined as any electronic mail message the primary purpose of which is the commercial advertisement or promotion of a commercial product or service, including email that promotes content on commercial websites. The law makes no exception for business-to-business email. Each separate email in violation of the CAN-SPAM Act is subject to penalties (the guide states up to 16,000 dollars per email; the statutory amount is periodically adjusted upward for inflation).

## The seven main requirements

1. Do not use false or misleading header information. Your From, To, Reply-To, and routing information, including the originating domain name and email address, must be accurate and identify the person or business who initiated the message.

2. Do not use deceptive subject lines. The subject line must accurately reflect the content of the message.

3. Identify the message as an ad. You must disclose clearly and conspicuously that your message is an advertisement.

4. Tell recipients where you are located. Your message must include your valid physical postal address (a current street address, a registered post office box, or a private mailbox).

5. Tell recipients how to opt out of receiving future email from you. Your message must include a clear and conspicuous explanation of how the recipient can opt out.

6. Honor opt-out requests promptly. You must honor an opt-out request within 10 business days. The opt-out mechanism must be able to process requests for at least 30 days after you send the message. You cannot charge a fee, require personally identifying information beyond an email address, or make the recipient take any step other than sending a reply email or visiting a single web page.

7. Monitor what others are doing on your behalf. If you hire another company to handle your email marketing, both the company that promotes the product and the company that actually sends the message may be held legally responsible.

## Note versus GDPR

CAN-SPAM is opt-out based (you may email until asked to stop) whereas GDPR (EU) is opt-in / consent based. A global sender must satisfy the stricter of the two per audience.

title: Google, Postmaster Tools dashboards (spam rate, reputation, authentication)
text:
## Spam Rate

Measures the percentage of messages recipients manually mark as spam in Gmail after inbox delivery. The dashboard reflects user-reported spam only, not messages Gmail automatically filters. Per Google's bulk-sender guidelines the target is under 0.10% and never at or above 0.30%.

## Domain and IP Reputation

Both dashboards rate sending quality across four categories.

Bad: history of sending a high volume of spam regularly. Email from this domain or address is almost always marked as spam or rejected by the receiving server.

Low: history of sending a significant volume of spam regularly. Email from this domain or address is likely to be marked as spam.

Medium: history of sending legitimate email, but occasionally sends spam. Most email has a fair deliverability rate, except when there is a notable increase in spam.

High: history of very low spam rates, and complies with Gmail's sender guidelines. Email from this domain or address is rarely marked as spam by Gmail.

## Feedback Loop (FBL)

Displays spam reporting data for campaign messages that carry feedback-loop identifiers. Shows the average FBL spam rate over time and unique campaign identifier volume, with aggregation by From-header domain or by DKIM signer.

## Authentication

Reports success percentages for SPF, DKIM, and DMARC on messages containing your sending domain in the From header. Well-configured senders typically see 95% or higher pass rates.

## Encryption and Delivery Errors

Encryption shows the percentage of authenticated messages carried over secure TLS connections (inbound and outbound). Delivery Errors shows rejection and temporary-failure rates with specific failure reasons, useful for diagnosing rate limiting or blocks.

title: Validity, What Is a Spam Trap? (types and avoidance)
text:
## Definition

Spam traps are email addresses designed to identify senders who practice poor list hygiene. They look like ordinary addresses but exist only to catch senders who are not following permission-based practices. Because major mailbox providers and blocklist operators monitor them, hitting one signals that your list contains addresses you never had permission to mail.

## Three types of spam traps

Typo traps result from user input errors during registration, such as an extra character (newsubscriber@yahooo.com) or Gail.com instead of Gmail.com. They are the easiest to prevent through real-time address validation at the point of capture.

Recycled traps, also called honeypots, were once legitimate addresses that mailbox providers reclaimed after roughly 12 or more months of inactivity, then repurposed as traps. They surface when senders keep mailing outdated lists or buy third-party data. Hitting them proves you are not sunsetting inactive contacts.

Pristine traps are fabricated addresses never intended for a real subscriber, created solely to be used as traps, then left in the wild to be scraped from websites, purchased, and passed around. They pose the greatest reputational risk because their presence proves the address could only have arrived via scraping or a purchased list, never via opt-in.

## How senders hit them

Purchasing email lists with unverified addresses; lacking documented subscriber consent; neglecting list hygiene and validation; and failing to remove inactive subscribers before they become recycled traps.

## Consequences and avoidance

Hitting traps can get domains or IPs blocklisted (for example by Spamhaus), send mail automatically to the spam folder, and damage sender reputation with mailbox providers. Avoid them by never purchasing lists, implementing double opt-in confirmation, validating addresses with software, removing inactive subscribers through re-engagement or sunset campaigns, and conducting regular list audits.

title: BIMI Group, Brand Indicators for Message Identification (BIMI) overview
text:
## What BIMI is

BIMI (Brand Indicators for Message Identification) enables authenticated senders to display their brand logo next to their emails in participating mailbox providers' inboxes, enhancing brand recognition and trust. The logo appears in the avatar slot of the inbox list.

## Prerequisite: DMARC enforcement

BIMI is built on top of email authentication. A sending domain must have a DMARC policy at enforcement (p=quarantine or p=reject), not merely p=none, before a BIMI logo can display. This is deliberate: only domains that have proven they control who sends as them earn the visible logo, so BIMI acts as an incentive to reach DMARC enforcement.

## Logo format

BIMI requires the logo in SVG Tiny Portable/Secure (SVG Tiny PS) format, a constrained square SVG profile. The BIMI Group provides an SVG Assistant and conversion tools to produce a compliant file. The logo should be a square, centered brand mark on a solid background.

## Verified Mark Certificate (VMC)

Some mailbox providers, notably Gmail and Apple, require a Verified Mark Certificate (VMC), a certificate issued by an authorized Certificate Authority that verifies the organization owns the trademarked logo. The VMC is referenced in the BIMI DNS record via the a= tag.

## DNS record and adoption

BIMI is published as a DNS TXT record (default selector at default._bimi.[domain]) pointing to the SVG logo (l= tag) and optionally the VMC (a= tag). Providers that support BIMI include Apple, Google, Yahoo, Fastmail, and others; Microsoft Outlook has historically not supported it. Net effect: BIMI rewards senders who complete SPF, DKIM, and DMARC-at-enforcement with a trust-building visible logo.

title: Mailchimp, Email Marketing Benchmarks by Industry
text:
## Overall benchmarks (all industries)

Across all Mailchimp users the averages are: open rate 35.63%, click rate 2.62%, and unsubscribe rate 0.22%. These are post-MPP figures, so open rate is inflated by Apple Mail Privacy Protection and should be read as directional.

## Selected industry benchmarks

Business and Finance: 31.35% open, 2.78% click, 0.15% unsubscribe.
Non-Profits: 40.04% open, 3.27% click, 0.18% unsubscribe.
Education and Training: 35.64% open, 3.02% click, 0.18% unsubscribe.
Ecommerce: 29.81% open, 1.74% click, 0.19% unsubscribe.

Ecommerce carries a notably lower click rate than content-led sectors like non-profits and education, a useful reminder that a healthy click rate is industry-relative, not absolute.

## Methodology

The analysis examined billions of emails delivered through Mailchimp where campaign tracking was on and industry was reported. Only campaigns reaching at least 1,000 subscribers were included, spanning organizations from startups to Fortune 500. Data last updated December 2023. Mailchimp notes that Apple's Mail Privacy Protection (MPP) affects open-rate accuracy.

## How to use benchmarks

Benchmarks set a reference band, not a target. Compare against your own industry row, watch trend over time within your own account, and never chase another sender's open rate given how MPP and list composition distort the number.

title: Klaviyo, Welcome Email Examples and Best Practices
text:
## Why welcome emails matter

The welcome series is the critical first touchpoint. It capitalizes on subscribers' highest engagement and purchase intent right after signup, so it consistently ranks among the highest-ROI automations a brand can run. The first email should deploy immediately after signup, while intent is at its peak.

## Structure and timing

Send across the roughly 10-day window when new subscribers are most likely to purchase, with at least one day between messages so you do not overwhelm them. Mix email types across the series: educational, offer-led, product-focused, and information-gathering (quiz or survey) messages.

## Key elements to include

Clear, personalized subject lines around 7 words; copy that answers what is in it for me; strong product imagery or video; a single strong call to action; a clear value proposition; the signup incentive or special offer promised at opt-in; an introduction to brand values; support contact details and a working unsubscribe; and opportunities to collect zero-party data via quizzes or surveys.

## Benchmark performance (Klaviyo 2025)

Welcome emails average a 51% open rate. Top-performing welcome emails reach a 15% click rate and a placed-order rate near 10%. Average revenue per recipient for the welcome series is about 2.35 dollars, far above a typical one-off campaign. These numbers explain why the welcome flow is treated as non-negotiable table stakes in lifecycle programs.

title: Klaviyo, Ecommerce Email Marketing Benchmark Report (flows vs campaigns)
text:
## Flows outperform one-off campaigns

Klaviyo's benchmark data shows automated flows (triggered by behavior) dramatically outperform broadcast campaigns on revenue per recipient, because a flow reaches a subscriber at the exact moment of intent. Campaigns sent to a narrow, well-segmented slice of the list outperform campaigns blasted to most of the list on open rate, click rate, and revenue per recipient, which is the quantitative case against batch-and-blast.

## Revenue per recipient by flow (average order size 100 to 200 dollars)

Abandoned cart: 7.01 dollars per recipient. Welcome series: 3.34 dollars per recipient. Browse abandonment: 1.95 dollars per recipient. Win-back: 0.84 dollars per recipient. The abandoned-cart flow is the single highest-earning automation because it catches a shopper who already chose a product.

## Scaling with order value

For stores with an average order size above 200 dollars, abandoned-cart revenue per recipient rises to 14.14 dollars, the highest performer in the study, showing that high-AOV catalogs get outsized returns from recovery flows.

## Aggregate impact

In the Q4 window studied, the companies generated over 230 million dollars in email-attributed purchases, roughly 27% of total store revenue, with automated flows alone bringing in over 50 million dollars. The strategic takeaway: build the core flow suite (welcome, abandoned cart, browse abandonment, post-purchase, win-back) before optimizing broadcast campaigns.

title: BigCommerce, Abandoned Cart Emails (best practices and timing)
text:
## Cart abandonment context

The global shopping cart abandonment rate reached 75.38% in 2025. Reasons for abandonment: 39% of shoppers cite extra costs (shipping, taxes, fees); 24% are discouraged by mandatory account creation; 17% abandon due to checkout complexity; and 43% say they are just looking or not ready to buy. This is why recovery emails work: most abandoners are recoverable, not lost.

## Recommended three-email sequence and timing

Email 1 within 1 to 3 hours, a friendly reminder showing the exact items. Email 2 within 24 hours, adding urgency or social proof. Email 3 within 48 to 72 hours, introducing an incentive only if needed. Sending the first email quickly, while intent is fresh, is the single biggest lever.

## Content of each email

Clear product images with pricing and variant details; a single prominent call-to-action button; a personalized subject line referencing the abandoned item; social proof such as ratings and reviews; support contact information; and one primary conversion goal per email.

## Subject lines and incentives

Personalized subject lines achieve roughly 46% open rates versus 35% without personalization, about a 31% relative improvement. On incentives: start with a plain reminder and introduce a discount only in the third email if the shopper still has not converted, so you avoid training customers to abandon carts on purpose to earn a coupon. High-performing abandoned-cart campaigns can generate double-digit conversion rates, among the most effective revenue-recovery strategies in ecommerce.

title: MailerLite, Email Accessibility Guide
text:
## Alt text and images

Include descriptive alt text for every meaningful image: instead of Image of a bear, write A brown bear walking in the forest. For purely decorative images that convey no information, use an empty alt tag (alt="") so screen readers skip them. Because many recipients and providers block images by default, the email must make sense with images off, so critical content should be live text, never baked into a single hero image.

## Semantic HTML structure

Use a proper heading hierarchy (h1, h2) so assistive technology can navigate by section rather than reading linearly. Apply role="presentation" to layout tables, which tells screen readers to ignore the table structure and read the content in a simple straight line. Declare the document language with <html lang="en"> so screen readers pronounce text correctly.

## Color and contrast

Maintain a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (14px bold or 18px). Links need at least 3:1 for larger or bold text. Never rely on color alone to convey meaning: instead of Click the red button, write Click the red button marked Continue so colorblind users understand.

## Typography and readability

Choose clean sans-serif fonts (Arial, Helvetica, Calibri, Verdana). Left-align body text rather than justifying it, since justification creates uneven spacing that hurts readability. Ensure adequate line height and spacing.

## Links, buttons, and interaction

Use descriptive link text (Read our latest guide on email accessibility) instead of click here. CTA buttons should state the outcome (Download Report, not Click Here). Mobile tap targets should be at least 24 by 24 pixels. Use a responsive single-column layout that reflows when zoomed to 400%.

## Plain text and why it matters

Always include a clean plain-text version carrying all the important information. Accessible design benefits everyone, not only people with disabilities: clear contrast, logical structure, and simple language help readers in a rush or reading on a phone in bright sunlight.

title: Litmus, Dark Mode Email Best Practices (resource hub)
text:
## Three ways clients handle dark mode

Email clients handle dark mode in three ways: some make no changes and render your email as built; some partially invert (reverse) your colors, flipping light backgrounds to dark while leaving already-contrasting colors alone; and some fully invert nearly every color, including ones you set deliberately. This is why the same email can look correct in one inbox and broken in another.

## Design for both modes up front

Approach dark mode during the design phase, not as an afterthought, because retrofitting a light-only design tends to break. Build the style system so every color, text block, and image works under both light and dark rendering. Favor midtones (grays and muted colors) over pure white or pure black, since extremes are what many clients auto-invert. A common safe pairing is dark gray text near #111111 on off-white near #F9F9F9, and near-white text on very dark gray for the dark variant.

## Logos and images

Dark logos or dark text baked into transparent PNGs can vanish on a dark background. The fix is to add padding, a subtle outline, or a solid background plate to keep the mark visible after inversion, and to test image rendering specifically.

## Coding and testing

Dark-mode control uses CSS such as the prefers-color-scheme media query plus color-scheme and supported-color-schemes meta tags; support varies (Apple Mail respects CSS overrides, while some Gmail and Outlook app contexts force-invert with limited CSS support). Because behavior differs by client and device, test on individual email clients and devices before every send using previews (for example Litmus or Email on Acid) that capture screenshots across dozens of clients in both light and dark modes.

title: GDPR.eu, GDPR consent and email marketing
text:
## Valid consent under GDPR

Consent for email marketing must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous. The request must be clearly distinguishable from other matters and written in clear, plain language. Organizations must keep documentary evidence (proof) of consent. Pre-ticked boxes are insufficient: consent requires an affirmative opt-in action by the individual. Children under 13 require parental permission.

## Right to withdraw consent

Individuals can withdraw previously given consent whenever they want, and you must honor that decision. You cannot circumvent a withdrawal by quietly switching to a different legal basis after the fact. It must be as easy to withdraw consent as it was to give it.

## Lawful basis for marketing email

There are two main pathways. Consent-based: obtain affirmative opt-in (no pre-ticked boxes). Legitimate-interest / existing-relationship (the ePrivacy soft opt-in): if you already provide a service to someone, you may market similar products provided customers are clearly and distinctly given the opportunity to object, free of charge and easily, both at collection and in every message. Every communication must include a clear unsubscribe option.

## Practical implication versus CAN-SPAM

GDPR is opt-in by default, the opposite of the US CAN-SPAM opt-out posture. A sender emailing EU or UK residents cannot rely on purchased lists or assumed consent; the burden of proof is on the sender to show valid, recorded consent for each contact.

title: Twilio SendGrid Docs, Warm Up an IP Address
text:
## What IP warmup is and why it is required

IP warmup means gradually increasing email volume through a new dedicated IP address. When an ISP observes email coming from an added or cold IP address, it begins evaluating the traffic from that IP. A brand-new IP has no reputation, so a sudden burst of high volume looks exactly like a spammer and gets throttled, deferred, or filtered to spam. Establishing a positive sender reputation takes less effort than repairing a damaged one, so warm up correctly the first time.

## Gradual ramp

The slower you can warm up, the better, because a slow ramp lets you locate and fix anomalies and issues as they appear rather than after damage is done. SendGrid provides an automated warmup schedule that escalates over roughly 40 to 41 days, starting very small (on the order of tens of emails per hour on day 1) and increasing exponentially day over day until it reaches full production volume, after which automated warmup concludes.

## Best-practice sequencing (industry consensus)

Start by sending to your most engaged recipients (recent openers/clickers), because their positive engagement teaches ISPs the IP is legitimate. Transactional mail, which recipients expect, is ideal early-warmup traffic. Keep the bounce rate low (under a few percent) and the spam-complaint rate under 0.1% throughout; a spike means slow down or pause. Never jump volume more than roughly 2x in a day.

## Consequences of skipping warmup

Skipping warmup, or buying/borrowing a cold or shared IP and blasting from it, triggers rate limiting, temporary blocks (deferrals), and spam-folder placement. If deliverability fails, SendGrid retries sending for up to 72 hours. Sending cold at full volume is one of the classic deliverability anti-patterns: the reputation hit can take weeks to undo.

title: Mailchimp, The Effects of List Segmentation on Email Marketing Stats
text:
## The study

Mailchimp analyzed roughly 2,000 users who sent about 11,000 segmented campaigns to nearly 9 million recipients, comparing segmented sends against those same senders' non-segmented sends. This is the canonical quantitative case for segmentation over batch-and-blast.

## Segmented versus non-segmented (overall)

Opens 14.31% higher; unique opens 10.64% higher; clicks 100.95% higher (roughly double); bounces 4.65% lower; abuse (spam) reports 3.90% lower; unsubscribes 9.37% lower. Segmentation improves engagement and simultaneously reduces the exact signals (complaints, unsubscribes, bounces) that damage deliverability.

## By segmentation method

By merge field: clicks +54.79%, opens +14.06%, unsubscribes -7.19%. By signup date: clicks +51.64%, opens +29.56%, but bounces +55.18% (older addresses added earlier bounce more, a hygiene warning). By interest group: clicks +74.53%, abuse reports -17.78%, unsubscribes -25.65%. By subscriber activity (engagement): unique opens +12.23%, clicks +15.69%, bounces -9.23%.

## Conclusion

Segmenting has an overwhelmingly positive impact on subscriber engagement. The strongest levers are interest-group and activity-based segmentation, which raise clicks while cutting complaints and unsubscribes, the opposite of what batch-and-blast to the whole list produces.

title: Klaviyo, What Is Sunsetting in Marketing (sunset policy)
text:
## What sunsetting is

Sunsetting is phasing out and removing chronically inactive subscribers from your email or SMS list. It is a core list-hygiene discipline: a large tail of people who never open drags down your engagement rates, and because mailbox providers increasingly filter on engagement, unengaged contacts pull your whole list toward the spam folder and can hit recycled spam traps.

## Why it protects the whole program

Removing inactive subscribers can increase click rates and purchasing by ensuring only engaged subscribers receive content. Keeping high volumes of non-responsive contacts risks deliverability problems: unengaged addresses can trigger spam filters and ROI can plummet. In other words, a smaller engaged list outperforms a larger dead one, which is why never sunsetting is an anti-pattern.

## Defining inactivity

Klaviyo suggests segmenting inactive users into categories such as: never active (no opens or purchases in the last 180 days); unengaged and never purchased (no opens in 180 days despite prior engagement); and unengaged but past purchaser (no purchases in 60 days and no opens in 180 days). Tune these windows to your normal purchase cycle.

## Win-back before removal

Before suppressing anyone, attempt re-engagement: send a short win-back sequence (a reminder, a value message, and an incentive or exclusive offer). Subscribers gave consent and may re-engage with a good offer. Those who still do not engage should be suppressed.

## Suppress, do not delete

Use suppression rather than deletion for sunset contacts, so you keep the record (and consent history) and avoid re-adding them later. Automate this with a sunset flow so hygiene runs continuously rather than as a one-off cleanup.

title: Litmus, The Anatomy of a Good Email (from name, subject line, preheader, CTA)
text:
## From name (sender name)

The from name drives the open decision as much as the subject line, because recipients scan who it is from first. Use a recognizable company name or a person your audience actually knows and trusts. Avoid no-reply addresses: no-reply signals that the recipient's feedback is not welcome, which harms the relationship and can hurt deliverability. A recipient who replies also generates a positive engagement signal.

## Subject line

Write in a conversational tone, like messaging a colleague, not legal boilerplate. Front-load the critical information because mobile clients truncate: make the first 35 to 40 characters hook the reader. Prefer direct over vague (Ready to triple response rates? beats Do not miss this). Use smart personalization beyond a first name, such as job title or a past purchase. Personalized subject lines lift open rates meaningfully.

## Preheader (preview text)

The preheader is the co-pilot to the subject line and extends the conversation. Most inboxes start truncating preheaders around 35 to 75 characters, so keep it tight. Do not repeat the subject line: add new value, answer the implied question, or state the payoff. If you leave the preheader empty, clients pull stray text (like View in browser), which wastes the slot.

## Single clear call to action

Give each email one primary call to action. Use a button rather than a bare hyperlink, especially on mobile, and write action-oriented copy naming the outcome (Download the guide, Try the demo) rather than Click here.

## Live text, images, and mobile

Do not build an image-only email: not everyone sees images (image blocking, accessibility), so the message must stay coherent with images off, and every image needs alt text. Use a single-column responsive layout, real heading tags (H1, H2, H3) for structure, and short one to two sentence paragraphs. Test on real devices and A/B test subject lines, layouts, and send times.

title: IETF RFC 8058, Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Email Headers
text:
## What one-click unsubscribe is

RFC 8058 defines the one-click unsubscribe that Gmail and Yahoo now require of bulk senders. It uses two coordinated headers so a recipient can unsubscribe with a single click on the mailbox provider's native Unsubscribe button, without opening the message or landing on a page.

## The two headers

List-Unsubscribe MUST contain one HTTPS URI (it may also contain a mailto: URI). List-Unsubscribe-Post is a new header with the fixed value List-Unsubscribe=One-Click. The presence of List-Unsubscribe-Post is what signals one-click capability to the mail client.

## Operational flow

A mail client that recognizes these headers performs an automated HTTPS POST to the URL in List-Unsubscribe, sending the key-value pair List-Unsubscribe=One-Click in the request body. The POST content should be sent as multipart/form-data or may be application/x-www-form-urlencoded. On receiving it, the sender must unsubscribe the address (Gmail and Yahoo require processing within 2 days).

## Why POST, not GET

Anti-spam software and mailbox scanners often auto-fetch every URL in the header via GET. By requiring an explicit POST triggered by user action, the mechanism prevents scanners from accidentally unsubscribing people during routine scanning.

## Authentication requirement

The message must carry a valid DKIM signature that covers both the List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post headers, so the sender takes responsibility for the request and spoofing is prevented. Note this one-click header is separate from, and required in addition to, a visible unsubscribe link in the body.

title: Litmus, Single Opt-In vs Double Opt-In
text:
## Definitions

Single opt-in (SOI): a contact joins after one step, usually submitting an email via a form, and is added immediately without confirmation. Double opt-in (DOI), also called confirmed opt-in: after signup the subscriber must click a confirmation link sent to their address before being officially added.

## Benefits of double opt-in

Verified addresses and reduced bounces, because confirmation proves the mailbox exists and is reachable. Fewer spam complaints, because you end up with a list full of people who actively agreed to be there. GDPR compliance, because the confirmation click is documented, auditable proof of consent. Higher engagement, because confirmed subscribers are more motivated. Double opt-in also filters out typo spam traps and malicious signups before they ever enter the list.

## The tradeoff

Some subscribers never complete the confirmation step, so a double opt-in list grows more slowly than a single opt-in list. That lost fraction is the real cost of the method.

## When each makes sense

Use single opt-in when you prioritize rapid list growth and can closely monitor deliverability metrics. Use double opt-in when you want a smaller, higher-quality, verified, engaged base or must prove consent under privacy regulations. There is no single best opt-in strategy; the right choice depends on business priorities. Note that mailbox providers like Yahoo explicitly recommend double opt-in, and it is the safest default for cold or high-risk acquisition sources.
